targets.problem: There is no reliable way to forecast the maximum magnitude of an earthquake induced by fluid injection, which is the binding regulatory question for CO2 storage, enhanced geothermal and wastewater disposal. Volume-based bounds (McGarr-type), pressure-perturbed-fault-area bounds and extreme-value statistics disagree; a 2026 global compilation finds the standard Gutenberg-Richter extrapolation fails in about half of induced sequences, and the 'traffic light' protocols in regulation rest on empirical correlations that lose sensitivity to injection volume over time. Also unresolved: whether cyclic or rate-modulated injection actually reduces Mmax.
targets.notes: B-terms to bridge through: pore-pressure diffusion vs poroelastic stress transfer at distance; the distinction between a pressure front and fluid particle travel (the same split as hydrology's old-water problem); hydraulic diffusivity and its stress dependence; fault-zone storativity; aseismic slip loading a locked patch; and whether seismicity tracks injected volume or pressurized area. OLD vocabulary: 'water flooding', 'pressure maintenance', 'secondary recovery', 'injectivity index', 'pressure transient / build-up and fall-off analysis', 'parting pressure' and 'formation breakdown pressure', 'thief zones' and 'channeling', 'sweep efficiency', 'interference testing', 'rock bursts' and 'bumps' (mining), 'reservoir-induced seismicity' (dam literature), 'subsidence and fluid withdrawal'. Cross-field literatures: petroleum reservoir engineering 1930s-1975 (AIME/SPE Transactions, Muskat, Hubbert-Rubey, Matthews-Russell pressure build-up monographs) which measured in-situ pressure diffusion and parting pressures in thousands of wells; U.S. Bureau of Mines rock-mechanics and rock-burst reports; the 1960s-1970s Rangely and Rocky Mountain Arsenal experiments and their contemporaneous but separate hydrological reports; Soviet and Indian dam-impoundment seismicity literature (Nurek, Koyna) often untranslated; and salt-solution-mining and gas-storage cavern engineering. Traps: Rocky Mountain Arsenal and Rangely are the canonical story — do not propose them as the rediscovery. Avoid re-litigating Oklahoma wastewater, which is heavily data-mined. The useful, unmined asset is the pre-1975 well-by-well pressure-transient and parting-pressure data, which bounds in-situ hydraulic diffusivity and the pressurized area far better than any modern inference, and which seismology papers essentially never cite. || WHY OLD LIT: Modern Mmax models are limited by not knowing how large an area actually got pressurized, which is a hydraulic-diffusivity question. The oil industry answered that question field by field for half a century using interference and fall-off testing, under vocabulary ('pressure maintenance', 'injectivity', 'sweep') with no keyword overlap with induced seismicity. Those datasets also record the pressure at which formations start to part, which is precisely the threshold the traffic-light systems try to stay below. || HOW TO CHECK: (1) Compile pre-1975 waterflood pressure-transient and parting-pressure data for basins that later hosted induced sequences (Permian, Anadarko, Illinois, Alberta), derive independent hydraulic-diffusivity and pressurized-area estimates, and test the pressurized-area Mmax bound against the observed largest events — a computation against public state-agency and SPE archives. (2) If the old data say diffusivity in a given formation is much higher or lower than currently assumed, that is a direct, checkable correction to an operating traffic-light threshold: a document and database edit with immediate regulatory meaning. (3) Also checkable: whether the 1950s-1970s waterflood literature already contains the cyclic-vs-continuous injection comparison (it ran 'pulsed' and 'cyclic' floods for sweep reasons) and what it found about induced fracturing.
targets.domain: Earth science, geology, hydrology, seismology and climate

targets.problem: Observed ice-crystal number concentrations in mixed-phase clouds exceed measured ice-nucleating-particle (INP) concentrations by one to three orders of magnitude at temperatures warmer than about -15 C. Models constrained to measured INP underproduce cloud ice (documented for E3SM/CAM Arctic cases and in Southern Ocean clouds), which is a leading suspect in the long-standing Southern Ocean shortwave radiation bias and in Arctic cloud-phase errors. Secondary ice production is the favored explanation but its mechanisms and relative importance are stated in the literature to remain unknown, and most climate models do not represent it. Verified live via 2020-2025 model-evaluation and Southern Hemisphere INP papers.
targets.notes: B-terms to bridge through: rime splintering, droplet shattering on freezing, ice-ice collisional fragmentation, sublimation fragmentation, and the biological and mineral identity of warm-temperature INPs (soil organic matter, leaf-surface bacteria, pollen, fungal spores, feldspar in dust). OLD vocabulary: 'freezing nuclei' and 'sublimation nuclei', 'ice nucleus counter', 'threshold temperature of nucleation', 'silver iodide seeding yield', 'nucleus spectrum', 'splinter production', 'bacterial frost injury' and 'frost-nucleation-active bacteria', 'nucleation activity of soil' and 'leaf litter nuclei'. Cross-field and pre-1985 literatures: the operational cloud-seeding era (Project Cirrus, Project Whitetop, Project Skywater, Australian CSIRO Division of Radiophysics bulletins, Soviet and Israeli hail-suppression programs), which ran enormous numbers of ice-nucleus counter measurements and splinter-yield experiments; agricultural plant-pathology and frost-protection literature on ice-nucleation-active bacteria (Pseudomonas syringae / Erwinia) and on soil and plant-debris nuclei, 1960s-1980s, in Phytopathology and plant-science journals; food-science and cryobiology freezing literature; and the 1950s-1970s 'ice nucleus paradox' discussions (Mossop and colleagues) that were dropped rather than solved. Traps: Hallett-Mossop (1974) rime splintering is already in every model as an option — it is the baseline, not a find. The Schnell-Vali 1972-1976 soil/leaf-litter nuclei papers are semi-known; the deeper, unmined seam is the operational seeding-program technical reports and the agricultural frost literature, which contain quantitative nucleus spectra for specific materials never since re-measured. || WHY OLD LIT: Hundreds of millions of dollars of 1950s-1970s weather-modification programs produced ice-nucleus counts, splinter-yield measurements and nucleus-source surveys that were published as agency technical reports and conference proceedings rather than indexed journal papers, then abandoned when seeding fell out of favor — they are poorly digitized and almost uncited by the modern INP community. In parallel, agricultural scientists characterized warm-temperature biological ice nucleators in quantitative detail for frost-protection reasons, in a literature with no citation overlap with atmospheric science. || HOW TO CHECK: Unusually direct. (1) Pick specific materials named in the old literature as unusually active at warm temperatures (particular soil fractions, leaf-litter extracts, named bacterial or fungal strains, specific mineral dusts) and re-run them in a modern droplet-freezing assay or continuous-flow diffusion chamber; a few weeks of standard lab work, and the result is a number that is right or wrong. (2) If an old splinter-yield or fragmentation-rate measurement differs from the one models use, implement it as a parameterization in an existing single-column or regional model and test whether Arctic phase partitioning and the Southern Ocean shortwave bias improve. (3) Database edit: add any confirmed nucleator to the community INP parameterization datasets.
targets.domain: Earth science, geology, hydrology, seismology and climate

targets.problem: Catchments discharge mostly pre-event water within minutes to hours of rainfall, yet mean transit times inferred from tritium and stable isotopes are years to decades. Thirty years after the isotope-hydrograph-separation debate, there is still no agreed physical mechanism for how a catchment instantaneously mobilizes old storage, and no predictive way to say which catchments will do it or how strongly. This blocks practical forecasting of storm-driven nitrate, phosphorus, DOC and legacy-contaminant delivery, and of how fast a catchment will respond to land-use or pollution change. Verified live: travel-time-distribution papers, the 2018 Erlenbach studies, and ongoing tritium work all still pose it as an unresolved paradox.
targets.notes: B-terms to bridge through: the distinction between a pressure/celerity response and a water-particle/velocity response; piston or translatory flow; transmissivity feedback as the water table reaches a more conductive horizon; preferential flow through macropores, root channels and soil pipes; capillary-fringe collapse (a small recharge flipping a near-saturated fringe into water-table rise); and air entrapment resisting infiltration. OLD vocabulary: 'translatory flow' and 'piston flow', 'tile drainage' and 'under-drainage', 'the Lisimeter/lysimeter', 'drainage coefficient', 'soil pipes' and 'crayfish burrows', 'non-capillary porosity', 'air entrapment' / 'air encapsulation', 'Horton overland flow' vs 'subsurface stormflow', 'Bodenwasserbewegung', 'karst conduit vs diffuse flow'. Cross-field and pre-1985 literatures: Victorian and early-20th-century agricultural drainage experiments (Rothamsted drain-gauge records from the 1870s onward are among the longest continuous drainage time series in existence, and the 1882 Lawes-Gilbert-Warington drainage work explicitly described water being pushed out ahead of new rain); mid-century soil physics and irrigation engineering (USDA and Agricultural Research Service soil-physics bulletins, Hungarian/Dutch/German land-drainage literature); petroleum reservoir engineering's pressure-front-vs-fluid-front distinction; karst hydrogeology and water-supply spring-chemistry monitoring (which tracked 'old' spring water responding instantly to rain long before isotope hydrology existed); and 1950s-1970s civil-engineering sewer and groundwater infiltration studies. Traps: Hewlett and Hibbert, Horton, and the McDonnell-Kendall 1992 exchange are the canonical frame — not a rediscovery. Do not propose 'macropores' generically; that is already standard. The lead worth chasing is specific quantitative drainage and chloride/nitrate-displacement datasets from pre-isotope agricultural drainage experiments that implicitly separate hydrographs by solute and were never re-analyzed as transit-time data. || WHY OLD LIT: Agricultural drainage engineers measured drain discharge and drainage-water chemistry continuously for a century because crops and fertilizer economics depended on it, and they described displacement of resident soil water by new rain in plain mechanical terms. That literature predates and does not share vocabulary with isotope hydrology, so it is nearly absent from the old-water citation network, yet it contains exactly the kind of paired flow-and-solute records needed to test competing transit-time models — on timescales no modern tracer study can match. || HOW TO CHECK: (1) Recover the long drainage records (Rothamsted drain gauges, USDA ARS watershed and lysimeter archives, Dutch and German land-drainage experiment stations), digitize paired discharge and solute-concentration series, and fit modern StorAge-Selection / travel-time-distribution models to them; this is a direct, checkable test of whether a specific old mechanism (e.g. capillary-fringe collapse, air-entrapment-driven piston displacement) reproduces the observed old-water fractions. Mostly archival plus computation. (2) If a mechanism survives, it predicts a measurable signature — e.g. a specific lag between water-table rise and tracer breakthrough — testable with a sprinkler or tracer experiment on an instrumented hillslope, which many observatories already have. (3) Deliverable is also a dataset contribution: century-scale drainage records added to the transit-time benchmark collections.
targets.domain: Earth science, geology, hydrology, seismology and climate

targets.problem: Accelerated silicosis in engineered/artificial-stone benchtop workers (and the Appalachian coal PMF resurgence) has no disease-modifying therapy and no secondary prophylaxis: once dust exposure stops, fibrosis still progresses. The specific stuck question is whether any inhaled or oral agent can blunt progression in a worker already diagnosed with simple silicosis — current practice is surveillance, transplant referral, and an unproven whole-lung-lavage program.
targets.notes: B-terms to bridge through: (1) 'aluminium prophylaxis' / 'McIntyre powder' / 'aluminium lactate inhalation' — finely milled aluminium dust was inhaled by tens of thousands of Ontario, Quebec and Cornish miners c.1943-1979 as a silica prophylactic, with animal evidence that Al blocks the silanol surface of quartz; the modern literature cites McIntyre powder almost exclusively as a neurotoxicity scandal, not as a dose-response dataset on silicotic progression. (2) 'poly-2-vinylpyridine-N-oxide' (PVNO, Bayer P204) — tested in German, Japanese and South African coal/gold miners in the 1960s-70s with reported radiographic benefit; vocabulary 'quartz surface masking', 'polyvinylpyridin-N-oxid'. (3) 'tetrandrine' / 'Han-fang-chin' / 'Stephania tetrandra' — approved in China for silicosis since the 1980s; the pre-1985 Chinese-language trial literature is essentially uncited in Western pneumoconiosis reviews. Dig in: Ontario Mining Association / Workmen's Compensation Board reports, Beiträge zur Silikoseforschung, Arbeitsmedizin journals, South African Pneumoconiosis Research Unit annual reports, Chinese Journal of Industrial Hygiene pre-1985. Traps: McIntyre records are an occupational-cohort goldmine (the MPEP cohort still exists and has been re-studied for neuro outcomes), so a lead there is an epidemiological re-analysis, not a new claim; do not confuse 'prevents silicosis incidence' with 'slows established disease'; aluminium inhalation has real neurotoxicity so any lead must be framed as mechanism-transfer (surface passivation) rather than reviving McIntyre powder itself. Sanity-checked: 2025 sources confirm no proven disease-modifying therapy; whole-lung lavage (SHIELD, NCT05402176) showed only a small 6-month CT-score change with no spirometry/DLCO benefit, and the one 2025 tetrandrine cohort is retrospective and uncontrolled — so the question is genuinely open, not settled. || WHY OLD LIT: Silica-surface pharmacology was an industrially funded, heavily published field from roughly 1940 to 1980 (aluminium therapy, PVNO, surface-charge/silanol masking) that was abandoned for reasons unrelated to efficacy: the Al programs collapsed over neurotoxicity fears and litigation, PVNO over a drug-development economics decision, and the whole subject vanished when Western mining shrank. The new engineered-stone epidemic is being worked by respirologists and ILD trialists who cite post-2000 fibrosis biology (IPF drugs, NLRP3) and almost never the pre-1985 dust-surface-chemistry literature, which sits in compensation-board reports and German/Japanese/Chinese journals that are not in the citation graph. || HOW TO CHECK: Cheap and layered. (a) Document check: locate the original PVNO and aluminium-therapy trial reports and tabulate radiographic progression endpoints — pure archival work. (b) Database/epi check: re-analyse the McIntyre Powder Project cohort for silicosis progression endpoints (exposure records and the MPEP intake clinic data already exist), low cost, no new subjects. (c) Bench check: a surviving surface-passivation lead can be tested on freshly fractured engineered-stone dust in a macrophage NLRP3/IL-1beta assay plus a 12-week rat intratracheal instillation model — on the order of tens of thousands of dollars and months, not years.
targets.domain: Public health, epidemiology, nutrition and occupational medicine

targets.problem: CKDu / Mesoamerican nephropathy: tens of thousands of young male agricultural workers in Central America, Sri Lanka and India develop tubulointerstitial kidney disease with no diabetes, hypertension or glomerular cause. Competing hypotheses (heat stress plus volume depletion, agrochemicals, heavy metals, leptospirosis, silica) have been chased for twenty years without resolution, and no preventive intervention beyond water-rest-shade has been validated. The precise stuck sub-problem: which exposure produces the distinctive tubular-atrophy-plus-interstitial-fibrosis lesion, and is there an existing occupational analogue whose dose-response is already published?
targets.notes: B-terms to bridge through: (1) 'nephropathia epidemica' / 'tubulointerstitial nephritis of the tropics' / 'heat nephritis' — a real pre-1960 clinical entity in stokers, boiler-room workers, Indian and Egyptian labourers, described in journals like the Indian Medical Gazette and the Journal of Industrial Hygiene with urinary findings strikingly like CKDu. (2) 'silica nephropathy' / 'silicon nephrolithiasis' / Russian-language 'silikoz pochki' — Soviet and Eastern-bloc occupational medicine reported renal lesions in silica-exposed workers; Central American cane and Sri Lankan farm work both involve high respirable/ingested silica and amorphous silica from cane ash, and nephrology does not cite this body of work. (3) 'Balkan endemic nephropathy' — the only prior endemic tubulointerstitial nephropathy ever solved (aristolochic acid), whose 1960s-70s investigative playbook (well-water organics, Pliocene lignite, mycotoxins, household clustering) was abandoned mid-way with many measured-but-unexplained findings still in print. (4) 'ochratoxin A' and 'fumonisin' in maize staples — food-science and veterinary (porcine nephropathy) literatures with quantitative renal dose-response that the CKDu literature barely touches. Dig in: pre-1970 tropical-medicine and industrial-hygiene journals, Soviet gigiena truda, veterinary nephrotoxicology, sugar-industry trade medicine. Traps: heat-stress work is now well funded and partly data-mined (so bring something it is not doing, e.g. the cane-ash silica or veterinary mycotoxin dose-response); and 'already solved' claims in reviews are usually hypothesis statements — check whether an intervention trial exists. Sanity-checked: 2025 case reports and 2020-2026 reviews still list four or more competing hypotheses with no consensus and no specific treatment, so the problem is live. || WHY OLD LIT: The investigators are nephrologists and climate-health epidemiologists working post-2002 with modern biomarker tools; their citation base starts around 2000. The closest analogues — colonial-era heat nephritis in labourers, Soviet occupational silica nephropathy, and the veterinary mycotoxin nephropathies — sit in three literatures (pre-1960 tropical medicine, Russian-language industrial hygiene, veterinary toxicology) that have essentially zero citation overlap with the CKDu corpus, partly for language and partly for disciplinary reasons. || HOW TO CHECK: Very checkable. Stored biospecimens from the MANOS cohort and the Sri Lankan CKDu cohorts can be assayed for whatever marker an old lead names (urinary silicon, ochratoxin A adducts, specific tubular markers) for a few tens of dollars a sample; cane-ash and well-water samples can be re-analysed directly. A veterinary dose-response lead is testable in an existing rodent model in under six months. An archival lead alone (matching a pre-1960 heat-nephritis case series' urinary and biopsy phenotype to the modern lesion) is a free document check that would redirect a large funded field.
targets.domain: Public health, epidemiology, nutrition and occupational medicine

targets.problem: Welding-fume and ferroalloy manganese parkinsonism has no accepted treatment: it responds poorly to levodopa, and whether chelation helps is unsettled — occupational medicine reviews variously claim good response to EDTA or PAS and failure to achieve sustained response. With manganese exposure rising again (electric-arc welding, Mn-rich battery chemistries, Mn fuel additive MMT, metal recycling) and no trial, clinicians have nothing to offer an affected worker.
targets.notes: B-terms to bridge through: (1) 'para-aminosalicylic acid' / 'PAS-Na' / 'sodium para-aminosalicylate' as a manganese chelator — Chinese occupational-medicine groups used intravenous PAS-Na courses in ferroalloy and mine workers from the 1970s onward with reported clinical and urinary-Mn responses; this literature is mostly Chinese-language and pre-1990. (2) 'chronic manganese poisoning' / 'manganese madness' / 'locura manganica' — the Chilean mine cohorts (Rodier 1955, Mena et al. 1960s) contain detailed natural-history and levodopa-response data, including claims of partial reversibility, that modern reviews cite only in passing. (3) 'CaNa2EDTA mobilisation' dosing protocols from lead medicine, and the Georgian/Soviet ferroalloy literature on 'manganotoxicosis'. (4) Veterinary and animal-nutrition literature on manganese-iron antagonism and on pharmacologic iron/calcium loading to reduce Mn uptake via DMT1 — animal science published quantitative antagonism data decades before the transporter was named. Dig in: Chinese Journal of Industrial Medicine and provincial occupational-disease journals pre-1990, Chilean and Soviet occupational neurology, pre-1985 animal-nutrition journals. Traps: the US welding-rod litigation (2003-2010) generated advocacy documents on both sides — treat Duke-style litigation reports as claims needing the primary trial data behind them, not as evidence; also distinguish chelation lowering body burden from chelation improving neurologic outcome, since Mn neurotoxicity may be irreversible once the globus pallidus is damaged. Sanity-checked: searching this turned up directly contradictory statements in the current literature (readily responsive to EDTA or PAS vs. failure to sustain response) with no controlled trial data surfacing — which is itself the evidence that the question is live and that the primary source material is uncited. || WHY OLD LIT: The problem's modern owners are movement-disorder neurologists and metal-transporter molecular biologists whose literature begins in the 1990s; the therapeutic trials, such as they are, were done 1955-1990 in Chile, China and the USSR, published largely outside English, and were never indexed in a way that survives into current reviews. Meanwhile the animal-nutrition field quantified Mn-Fe-Ca absorptive antagonism for livestock feed formulation and never framed it as therapy. || HOW TO CHECK: Document-level first: recover and translate the Chinese PAS-Na series and the Chilean cohort papers and extract actual endpoints and dosing — that alone resolves a contradiction currently sitting in review articles and is near-free. Then a surviving lead is checkable in the established Mn-exposed-rodent or non-human-primate T1-MRI model within months, and a protocol with pre-1985 human dosing already in hand is an unusually short path to a small open-label trial in an exposed workforce (ferroalloy plants with occupational-health departments exist and already do surveillance).
targets.domain: Public health, epidemiology, nutrition and occupational medicine

targets.problem: Kashin-Beck disease — endemic deforming osteochondropathy in Tibet, Qinghai, Siberia and formerly North Korea — still has no agreed cause after a century. Selenium deficiency, grain-borne T-2 toxin and drinking-water organics are each supported by associations and none by a decisive test; a 2024 Tibet study found high T-2 in brick tea rather than in the grain staple everyone suspected. Without an identified agent, prevention is guesswork even as the endemic areas change diet.
targets.notes: B-terms to bridge through: (1) the Russian-language corpus from 1849 onward — 'urovskaya bolezn' (Urov disease), named for the Urov river, with Soviet hydrogeochemistry and water-humic/fulvic-acid hypotheses, phosphorus and strontium-barium imbalance work, and decades of field surveys that Chinese and Western KBD papers cite only by name. (2) 'fluorosis of cartilage' / 'strontium rickets' — pre-1985 bone-pathology literature on Sr/Ca substitution and on skeletal fluorosis presents epiphyseal lesions resembling KBD; the Sr-rickets literature is 1950s-60s and sits in bone physiology, not endemic-disease, journals. (3) veterinary 'tibial dyschondroplasia' and 'degenerative joint disease' in Se-deficient or Fusarium-fed livestock — animal science quantified Se x mycotoxin x cartilage interactions commercially, with dose-response data, and does not cite KBD. (4) 'rhodanese', 'thiocyanate', and tea-borne fluoride/aluminium — the brick-tea finding should be cross-read against the large pre-1985 brick-tea fluorosis literature from Inner Mongolia and Siberia. Dig in: pre-1985 Soviet medical and hydrogeology journals, Japanese Manchurian-era surveys of KBD (1930s-40s, extensive and almost entirely uncited), veterinary nutrition. Traps: KBD incidence is falling for general-development reasons, so a confounded natural experiment is easy to over-read; several Chinese groups dominate the modern corpus, so independent-source leads matter; and Se deficiency is near-certainly a cofactor rather than the agent, so a lead that only re-proves low Se is worthless. Sanity-checked: the current literature explicitly states the precise aetiology is not clear and describes it as multifactorial, and the 2024 brick-tea T-2 result was reported as a first — so the field is unsettled and still finding basic exposure facts. || WHY OLD LIT: Two large bodies of original fieldwork — Soviet Urov-disease research (Russian, 1900s-1980s) and Japanese Manchurian-era surveys (Japanese, 1930s-40s) — were produced before the modern Chinese KBD program began, in languages and archives outside its citation graph, and they contain exposure measurements on waters, soils and grains in villages whose disease status was known. The veterinary cartilage literature independently quantified the exact Se-mycotoxin interaction now hypothesised, for reasons of poultry economics. || HOW TO CHECK: Highly checkable, and partly as a document/database task: the old Soviet and Japanese surveys name specific villages with specific water and soil chemistry and specific prevalence, so a lead becomes a geospatial cross-check against modern prevalence maps and archived water chemistry. A chemical lead (brick tea, a specific water organic, Sr/F) is directly measurable in current Tibetan samples for modest cost, and the Se-deficient-rat plus candidate-toxin cartilage model already exists and runs in weeks.
targets.domain: Public health, epidemiology, nutrition and occupational medicine

targets.problem: Occupational hearing-loss limits treat noise and chemicals separately: the 85 dB(A) criterion was derived for otherwise unexposed ears, and solvent/metal PELs were set without hearing endpoints. Animal and some human data indicate synergy at levels where neither agent alone is damaging, affecting an estimated 5-10 million US workers, yet no regulator has a combined-exposure criterion and NIOSH's own research agenda still lists adequate exposure limits for mixed exposures as an open need. The stuck sub-problem is quantitative: what is the interaction function, and does usable dose-response data already exist?
targets.notes: B-terms to bridge through: (1) Soviet and Eastern-bloc 'kombinirovannoe deistvie' / 'combined action of noise and chemical factors' — Soviet industrial hygiene made combined-factor hygienic norms an explicit research program from the 1960s and published quantitative interaction coefficients for noise with carbon disulphide, styrene, lead, vibration and heat, in Gigiena Truda i Professional'nye Zabolevaniya. Western mixed-exposure reviews cite essentially none of it. (2) 'carbon disulphide' viscose-rayon medicine, pre-1980 — the rayon industry's own medical departments recorded audiometry alongside CS2 exposure for decades in Italy, Japan, Poland and the UK. (3) 'carbon monoxide and noise' in the pre-1985 aviation-medicine and tunnel/garage-worker literature — CO potentiation of noise injury appears in aerospace physiology reports before it was rediscovered in the 1990s. (4) 'toluene abuse' neuro-otology, and veterinary/experimental 'cochlear hypoxia' work linking vasoconstrictive and oxygen-tension effects to temporary threshold shift. Dig in: Russian-language industrial hygiene, Polish Medycyna Pracy, Japanese Sangyo Igaku, rayon and rubber industry medical reports, early NASA/USAF aeromedical technical reports. Traps: mixed-exposure data are often confounded by co-exposure to the noise itself and by poor exposure measurement, so the prize is a dataset with independently measured chemical and noise exposures and audiometry — identify that before claiming a lead; also several EU countries and Australia already advise dropping to 80 dBA with ototoxicants, so the novelty must be the quantitative interaction, not the qualitative warning. Sanity-checked: NIOSH, AIHA and reviews from 2001-2019 confirm the gap is real and explicitly unresolved, and I found no 2024-2026 standard closing it. || WHY OLD LIT: Hearing conservation is a regulatory, English-language field whose evidence base is OSHA/NIOSH-era US and EU studies; the one research tradition that systematically studied combined physical-plus-chemical hygienic norms was Soviet, and it is effectively invisible to it. The industry medical archives (rayon, rubber, aviation) collected exactly the paired exposure-plus-audiometry data now wanted, for compensation purposes rather than science. || HOW TO CHECK: Unusually cheap to check because the deliverable can be a document or database artifact. A recovered Soviet interaction coefficient or an industry audiometry series can be tested against existing modern datasets — the Air Force maintenance-worker cohorts, NIOSH's Occupational Hearing Loss Surveillance database, and the large audiometric datasets US employers must keep — using exposure proxies by job title, i.e. pure re-analysis at near-zero marginal cost. An animal confirmation (rat, solvent plus noise, distortion-product otoacoustic emissions) is a standard few-month experiment. A confirmed interaction function is directly actionable as a proposed criterion change.
targets.domain: Public health, epidemiology, nutrition and occupational medicine

targets.problem: Konzo, the irreversible spastic paraparesis of bitter-cassava-dependent populations in DRC, Mozambique and Tanzania, is attributed to cyanogen exposure plus sulfur-amino-acid deficiency, yet the actual neurotoxic species and the reason for selective upper-motor-neuron damage are unidentified — recent experimental work explicitly failed to establish causation for cyanide or any previously hypothesised metabolite. Without the agent, prevention rests solely on wetting-method flour processing, and there is no treatment for the tens of thousands already affected.
targets.notes: B-terms to bridge through: (1) 'neurolathyrism' / 'lathyrus sativus' / 'beta-ODAP' / 'BOAA' — the sister disease, with a far older and much larger literature (Indian, Ethiopian, Spanish, and the 1940s-50s experimental work), including the classic 'detoxification by steeping' agronomy and the observation that outbreaks need famine plus a monotonous diet. Konzo and lathyrism papers overlap less than they should. (2) 'tropical ataxic neuropathy', 'Jamaican neuropathy' / 'tropical spastic paraplegia' pre-HTLV-1 — the 1950s-70s Nigerian, Jamaican and Indian literature on cyanide, thiocyanate and B12 in these syndromes was largely orphaned when HTLV-1 was discovered in 1980 and reclassified many cases; the cyanide-metabolism data in it were never followed up. (3) 'cyanate' and 'carbamylation' — carbamylation of proteins was characterised in detail by pre-1985 uremia and sickle-cell biochemistry (sodium cyanate was trialled as an anti-sickling drug and caused a dose-limiting peripheral and motor neuropathy in humans, with published dose-response and pathology). That human toxicology of cyanate is an almost perfect natural experiment that the konzo field cites only glancingly. (4) 'rhodanese', '3-mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase' and the amygdalin/laetrile toxicology of the 1970s, plus the ruminant 'cyanide-induced equine/caprine ataxia and sorghum cystitis-ataxia syndrome' veterinary literature, where selective spinal-cord lesions from cyanogenic forage were described and localised decades ago. Dig in: pre-1985 tropical neurology, the laetrile-era clinical toxicology, sickle-cell cyanate trials, and veterinary neuropathology of cyanogenic plant poisoning. Traps: do not re-propose plain cyanide (already excluded); the nutritional cofactor is accepted, so a lead must address agent identity or neuronal selectivity; and the famous konzo stories (wetting method, Howard Bradbury) are solved prevention, not the open mechanism. Sanity-checked: current and 2025 sources state neither the specific neurotoxic compound nor the pathogenic mechanisms have been elucidated, so this is live. || WHY OLD LIT: The sodium-cyanate anti-sickling trials of the 1970s produced detailed human dose-response neurotoxicity data that were published and then buried when the drug was abandoned; the veterinary sorghum/cyanogenic-forage literature localised selective spinal lesions for livestock-management reasons. Both are in clinical haematology and veterinary pathology, fields with no citation contact with African nutritional neurology, whose own corpus starts with the 1980s konzo outbreaks. || HOW TO CHECK: Concrete. A lead naming a specific species (cyanate carbamylation, a cystine-cyanide adduct such as 2-imino-4-thiazolidine carboxylic acid, a thiocyanate route) is measurable in stored konzo serum and urine specimens and in household flour, and carbamylated-protein assays are routine and inexpensive. Mechanistic confirmation uses the already-published SAA-deficient rat plus linamarin/cyanate model, weeks to months. Most cheaply, the 1970s human cyanate trial records give an existing dose-exposure-neuropathy curve that can be compared directly against estimated konzo exposures — a document and arithmetic check with no new experiment.
targets.domain: Public health, epidemiology, nutrition and occupational medicine

targets.problem: Short-pitch rail corrugation (roaring rails, 20-80 mm wavelength) still has no agreed formation mechanism, and models cannot predict which track sections will corrugate or reproduce initiation from nominal track parameters. Operators manage it only by periodic grinding. Specifically: identify the wavelength-fixing and amplitude-growth mechanism for cases where pinned-pinned resonance cannot apply (embedded rail / continuous support), and derive a track-design criterion (longitudinal fastening restraint, pad stiffness) that suppresses initiation.
targets.notes: Bridge B-terms: self-excited stick-slip oscillation; regenerative (surface-regenerative) instability with a delay term; frictional relaxation oscillation; differential wear vs. ratcheting plasticity; longitudinal creepage / torsional rail dynamics. OLD VOCABULARY to search: 'roaring rails', 'rail rippling', 'rail waving', 'wave formation on rails' (railway engineering 1900-1960, Engineering, Railway Gazette, ORE/UIC reports, JNR/RTRI Quarterly Reports, Soviet Vestnik and Zheleznye Dorogi); 'chatter' and 'regenerative chatter' in the 1950s-60s machine-tool literature (Tlusty, Tobias, Merritt, Doi & Kato) which formalised exactly the delay-differential surface-regeneration instability now rediscovered piecemeal in rail; 'brake squeal'/'stick-slip squeal' and 'frictional self-induced vibration' (Mills 1938, Bowden & Tabor, Rabinowicz's velocity-weakening friction, Sinclair 1955); 'washboarding'/'corrugation' on unpaved roads (soil mechanics and highway engineering, Mather 1963) and 'ripple formation' in grinding wheels and in snow/sand. ADJACENT NON-CITING FIELDS: machine-tool dynamics, earthquake/fault stick-slip (rate-and-state friction, pre-1985 rock mechanics), tribology of oxide third bodies. TRAP for a scout: huge modern literature exists, so only pre-1985 or non-rail sources count as finds; also do not confuse short-pitch corrugation with long-wave (roaring vs. rutting/heavy-haul) corrugation — separate phenomena with separate literatures, and papers often conflate them. || WHY OLD LIT: The phenomenon was described and instrumented from the 1900s onward in railway trade journals and national-railway research reports (JNR, ORE, Soviet, Deutsche Bundesbahn) that are mostly not digitised and almost never cited in modern vehicle-dynamics papers. Independently, the machine-tool chatter community solved the mathematics of surface-regenerative instability (delay equations, stability lobes, process damping) in 1954-1970 and that formalism is still not systematically applied to wheel-rail wear feedback. A quantitative stability-lobe criterion for corrugation may already exist in that vocabulary. || HOW TO CHECK: Cheap end: digitise field corrugation surveys from old railway reports and test whether a machine-tool-style stability-lobe criterion (built from published rail receptance and wear coefficients) retro-predicts which 1950s-60s sites corrugated. Mid cost: twin-disc rig (Sheffield-type) or full-scale roller rig experiment varying longitudinal fastener restraint and tangential creepage to test a predicted suppression condition. Expensive but decisive: instrumented track trial of a predicted fastening/pad configuration on a known corrugating curve.
targets.domain: Engineering: structures, transport, manufacturing, instrumentation and metrology

targets.problem: Multi-decade creep and shrinkage of concrete still cannot be predicted to better than roughly a factor of two, and the coefficient of variation of the leading code models (ACI 209, Eurocode/fib, AASHTO, B4) against the NU database remains 20-40%, which drives real failures: excessive long-term deflection of large-span prestressed box-girder bridges (Koror-Babeldaob class behaviour), prestress-loss underestimation, and nuclear containment tendon relaxation. Specifically: explain and parameterise the long-term (>10 yr) drying-creep divergence and the sealed-vs-drying creep split that no current model fits.
targets.notes: Bridge B-terms: microprestress relaxation; self-desiccation; moisture diffusion coupled to load (Pickett effect / drying-creep interaction); sorption hysteresis in nanopores; 'solidification' ageing; load-induced thermal strain. OLD VOCABULARY to search: 'plastic flow of concrete' and 'plastic yield' (the pre-1950 term for creep), 'time yield', 'deformation under sustained load'; US Bureau of Reclamation Boulder/Hoover and Grand Coulee dam concrete laboratory reports and Cement & Concrete Research Bulletins of the 1930s-50s; Glanville and Thomas (BRS, UK, 1930s), Davis & Davis (1931), Ross (1937), Lea & Lee, Hansen & Mattock (PCA, 1966), CEB 1970 bulletins, Soviet (Arutyunyan, Prokopovich, Aleksandrovskii) and Japanese literature; RILEM 1960s-70s symposium volumes. ADJACENT NON-CITING FIELDS: soil mechanics (Terzaghi/Taylor secondary consolidation, 'secular effect'), rheology of gels, wood and polymer creep (time-temperature-moisture superposition, moisture-change-accelerated creep - 'mechanosorptive creep' is a wood-science term with a large pre-1985 literature that concrete modelling barely cites), rock mechanics. TRAP: the NU/RILEM databases themselves are heavily mined; the find is not more data points but either (a) long-duration specimens physically still under load in old labs/dams with recoverable records, or (b) a constitutive form from mechanosorptive wood creep or soil secondary consolidation that already explains the drying-creep anomaly. Also beware the known early-time contamination of old creep curves (unrecorded time-zero, loading rate) - old records need the loading protocol documented or they are useless. || WHY OLD LIT: The only genuinely multi-decade creep measurements in existence were made between 1930 and 1970, by dam agencies and national building-research labs, in grey reports and in Russian/Japanese/German, using 'plastic flow' rather than 'creep' as the index term - so keyword-based database mining misses them, and the NU database draws mostly on what was convenient to digitise. Separately, wood science derived and validated a mechanosorptive constitutive law for moisture-cycling-driven creep decades ago; concrete models still treat drying-creep interaction phenomenologically. || HOW TO CHECK: Pure desk check with real teeth: digitise archival long-duration curves (Bureau of Reclamation, BRS, PCA, Soviet reports) with their loading protocols, then test whether current B4/fib/ACI models predict them and whether a mechanosorptive or secondary-consolidation functional form fits better; publishable with zero lab cost. Harder check: locate specimens still under sustained load (some 1960s RILEM and university racks survive) and take one reading. Field check: compare predictions against measured 40-year deflection histories of segmental box-girder bridges.
targets.domain: Engineering: structures, transport, manufacturing, instrumentation and metrology

targets.problem: Structural health monitoring of bridges, dams and offshore structures cannot separate genuine slow structural change from instrument drift: bonded foil and even FBG/printed sensors drift tens of microstrain over months, which is the same magnitude as the degradation signal being hunted over years. There is no accepted long-term-stable, traceable, self-checking static strain instrument for decade-scale deployment, and no standard drift-qualification protocol. Specifically: produce a static strain measurement chain with demonstrated sub-5-microstrain stability over 10 years, or an in-situ self-calibration method that bounds drift.
targets.notes: Bridge B-terms: zero-drift and creep of the gauge/adhesive/encapsulation stack; hydrogen and moisture ingress; differential thermal output ('apparent strain'); null-balance and substitution measurement; artefact-based in-situ recalibration; mechanical (not electrical) reference transfer. OLD VOCABULARY: 'Carlson elastic wire strain meter' (embedded in 1930s dams and still readable decades later - an existence proof of decade-scale stability that modern SHM papers almost never cite), 'vibrating wire extensometer', 'Whittemore gauge' and 'demountable mechanical strain gauge / DEMEC' (repeat-reading against a stable invar reference bar - a substitution method that is immune to electronic drift by construction), 'Berry strain gauge', 'Huggenberger tensometer', 'acoustic strain gauge' (pre-1960 Bureau of Reclamation/USACE and Japanese dam instrumentation), 'reference bar', 'gauge plug'. Search Bureau of Reclamation Concrete Laboratory reports, USACE Waterways Experiment Station, ACI Journal 1935-1965, the old Instrument Society of America transactions, Experimental Mechanics / Proceedings of SESA (Society for Experimental Stress Analysis) 1945-1980 on 'long-time stability of strain gauges', and NBS (now NIST) work on dimensional stability of metals and on 'secular change in gauge blocks' - metrology has a deep pre-1985 literature on long-term dimensional stability of invar/quartz/Zerodur that SHM does not read. ADJACENT NON-CITING FIELDS: geodetic/seismological instrumentation (laser and quartz-tube strainmeters, Benioff, Sacks-Evertson borehole dilatometers - the earth-strain community spent 1960-1985 explicitly characterising and defeating instrument drift at 1e-9 strain levels and published drift models), gauge-block and length metrology, precision resistor stability literature. TRAP: do not drift into vibration-based/modal SHM (saturated and heavily mined); this target is strictly static/quasi-static strain and displacement metrology. Also note printed and FBG sensor drift literature is recent and thin - that is the opportunity, not a reason to assume it is solved. || WHY OLD LIT: Dam engineers in the 1930s and earth-strain geophysicists in the 1960s both faced exactly this requirement (decade-scale absolute strain stability) and both solved substantial parts of it - by substitution measurement against a stable artefact, by embedded elastic-wire designs, and by published drift-separation models. SHM as a field dates its literature from the 1990s, uses different index terms ('sensor drift' vs 'secular instrument instability'), and cites essentially none of it; meanwhile NIST-lineage work on dimensional stability of low-expansion materials sits in a third silo. || HOW TO CHECK: Document check first: recover Carlson-meter and DEMEC long-term records from instrumented dams and show measured decade-scale stability figures - a database/document-level result. Then a cheap, decisive lab test: run a modern FBG/foil/printed sensor side by side with a reconstructed substitution-type mechanical gauge and an invar reference on an unloaded specimen in a controlled chamber for 6-12 months, and compare drift. Also directly checkable: whether the geophysical borehole-dilatometer drift-correction formalism, applied to existing published bridge monitoring datasets, removes the drift component.
targets.domain: Engineering: structures, transport, manufacturing, instrumentation and metrology

targets.problem: Life prediction for welded steel joints under real variable-amplitude service loading is still unreliable: the Palmgren-Miner damage sum at failure varies roughly 0.3-1.5 depending on load sequence and mean stress, so codes (IIW, Eurocode 3, FKM) simply cap D at 0.5 as a fudge. This governs remaining-life decisions for orthotropic steel bridge decks, cranes, offshore jackets and wind-turbine towers. Specifically: a validated sequence-sensitive damage rule for welded joints, replacing the linear sum, that works on measured service spectra without per-detail recalibration.
targets.notes: Bridge B-terms: load-sequence/interaction effects; crack-closure and overload retardation; residual-stress relaxation and shakedown under spectrum loading; cycle-counting and omission levels (what small cycles actually do); crack-growth threshold under variable amplitude. OLD VOCABULARY and literatures: German 'Betriebsfestigkeit' - Ernst Gassner's random/blocked-programme fatigue testing from 1939 onward, the 'Gassner line' (Gassnerlinie), LBF Darmstadt (Fraunhofer LBF) Berichte and Laboratorium fuer Betriebsfestigkeit reports, Buxbaum, Haibach's 'Betriebsfestigkeit' and his modified Miner rule, Schuetz - a very large pre-1985 German-language experimental corpus with service spectra (Gauss, Twist, Falstaff, Cold Turbistan) that English-language code work cites by name but has not re-mined for data; Dutch NLR work (Schijve, 1960s-70s, on sequence effects and crack closure); 'cumulative damage' conference volumes (ASTM STP 1960s-70s), 'programme loading' and 'flight-by-flight' full-scale aircraft test reports (NACA/NASA TN, RAE/ARL Technical Reports, Australian ARL) which contain thousands of variable-amplitude lives on welded and riveted details that modern damage-model papers never fit. ADJACENT NON-CITING FIELDS: aeronautical full-scale fatigue testing, railway axle and ship-hull fatigue (ship classification-society reports), Soviet fatigue literature. TRAP: the constant-amplitude S-N side is fully mined - do not go there. The find must be an old variable-amplitude dataset with the actual sequence documented, or an old nonlinear damage formulation (e.g. Corten-Dolan, Freudenthal-Heller interaction, Haibach's relative Miner) that already reproduces the modern scatter when properly applied. || WHY OLD LIT: Gassner-school Betriebsfestigkeit testing ran for forty years, in German, in institute report series with no DOIs, and produced precisely the sequence-resolved spectrum data that modern sequence-effect papers lack; similarly, NACA/RAE full-scale spectrum tests from 1945-1980 were published as grey technical notes. Both are effectively invisible to citation-graph and keyword mining, and the 0.5 damage cap in today's codes is the scar tissue from that disconnect. || HOW TO CHECK: Highly checkable and cheap: digitise sequence-documented variable-amplitude datasets from LBF/NACA/RAE reports and test candidate nonlinear damage rules against them out-of-sample - a pure computation plus document recovery. If a rule survives, confirm with a modest welded-specimen campaign using one old and one modern spectrum at the same rainflow content but different sequence (tens of specimens, standard rig). A surviving result is directly actionable as a code-revision proposal.
targets.domain: Engineering: structures, transport, manufacturing, instrumentation and metrology

targets.problem: Springback of advanced high-strength steel and aluminium stampings still cannot be predicted well enough to cut a die right the first time: dies are typically recut three to five times during tryout, and simulation error stems from poorly modelled unloading behaviour - nonlinear unloading, elastic (chord) modulus degradation up to ~10% plastic strain, Bauschinger transient softening and permanent softening. Specifically: a physically based unloading/reverse-loading model with parameters obtainable from standard tests, that predicts springback across grades and geometries without per-part calibration of an 'apparent modulus'.
targets.notes: Bridge B-terms: pseudo-elastic / anelastic strain recovery on unloading; internal (back) stress relaxation; dislocation pile-up bow-out and bauschinger transient; grain-boundary and twin-boundary internal stress; time-dependent room-temperature recovery and relaxation after unloading; residual-stress through-thickness distribution after bending-unbending. OLD VOCABULARY to search: 'anelasticity' and 'anelastic strain recovery' (Zener 'Elasticity and Anelasticity of Metals' 1948, Koester, Nowick & Berry 'Anelastic Relaxation in Crystalline Solids' 1972 - an entire pre-1985 physics literature on exactly the modulus-defect/strain-amplitude-dependent modulus phenomenon that sheet-forming now calls 'unloading modulus degradation'); 'modulus defect', 'Delta-E effect', 'internal friction' and 'damping capacity after plastic deformation' (Koehler, Granato-Lucke dislocation damping); Bauschinger 1886 and the German/Soviet 'Bauschinger-Effekt' literature; Masing's 1926 model of a composite of elastic-plastic elements (the original back-stress/kinematic-hardening idea), Besseling, Mroz multisurface; 'elastic aftereffect' / 'nachwirkung'; 1950s-70s roll-forming, tube-bending and press-brake handbooks and ASTIA/ASD reports on 'springback allowance' tables for maraging and high-strength sheet - the aerospace sheet-metal community generated large empirical springback datasets for very high-strength materials long before AHSS. ADJACENT NON-CITING FIELDS: internal-friction/anelasticity physics, geomechanics (hysteretic modulus degradation), civil engineering steel 'rounded-knee' stub-column work, precision-instrument spring design (pre-1985 horology and instrument-spring literature on hysteresis and drift in elastic elements). TRAP: springback simulation is a crowded modern field, so a lead only counts if it is pre-1985 or cross-field; also check that a candidate anelasticity model actually predicts the measured strain-dependence of the chord modulus, since several modern papers already fit curves to it empirically - the gap is physical parameterisation and prediction, not curve-fitting. || WHY OLD LIT: The anelasticity and internal-friction community characterised strain-amplitude- and plastic-prestrain-dependent modulus defects quantitatively, with dislocation-based models, in the 1940s-70s, under index terms ('modulus defect', 'anelastic relaxation', 'Delta-E effect') that no sheet-forming paper searches. Masing's 1926 composite model likewise predates and subsumes much of what is rediscovered as transient/permanent softening. The vocabularies never merged. || HOW TO CHECK: Immediately testable: standard cyclic tension-compression and loading-unloading-reloading tests on a DP/TRIP grade, compare measured chord-modulus-versus-prestrain and reverse-flow curves against the anelastic/dislocation-damping prediction (Granato-Lucke or Nowick-Berry form) rather than a fitted exponential; then plug the resulting model into the public NUMISHEET U-draw/bend and benchmark-part cases and compare springback error against the current apparent-modulus approach. Modest lab cost, public benchmarks for scoring, binary outcome.
targets.domain: Engineering: structures, transport, manufacturing, instrumentation and metrology

targets.problem: Residual stress and distortion in laser powder bed fusion and wire-arc AM remain a principal qualification barrier (stresses approaching yield, part cracking, build-plate warping, geometric non-conformance), and mitigation is almost entirely post-hoc: heat treatment, supports, compensation of the CAD geometry, or scan-pattern trial and error. Specifically: an in-process mechanical/thermal means of setting the inherent plastic strain field during deposition so the part comes out low-stress and dimensionally correct as built, with a design rule rather than per-part simulation.
targets.notes: Bridge B-terms: inherent strain / inherent shrinkage force; transient thermal tensioning; differential heating and trailing heat sink; mechanical tensioning and side-stretching; global vs local pre-stressing of the substrate; shakedown of transient plastic strain; vibratory stress relief; peening between layers. OLD VOCABULARY to search: 'low stress no distortion (LSND) welding' (Beijing Aeronautical Manufacturing Technology Research Institute, 1980s-90s), 'thermal tensioning' and 'differential heating' for thin-sheet welding, 'mechanical tensioning', 'trailing heat sink / cryogenic trailing cooling'; Okerblom's 'The Calculations of Deformations of Welded Metal Structures' (1955, Soviet - the original inherent-strain method, which modern AM 'inherent strain' solvers reinvent), Vinokurov 'Welding Stresses and Distortion' (Soviet, 1968), Masubuchi 'Analysis of Welded Structures' (1980) plus his MIT Sea Grant and shipyard reports, Paton Institute (Avtomaticheskaya Svarka / The Paton Welding Journal) 1960s-80s, Welding Research Council Bulletins, British Welding Journal, and shipbuilding-yard distortion-control practice (line heating, 'flame straightening' / Flammrichten, pre-cambering) which was quantitatively engineered pre-1985. ADJACENT NON-CITING FIELDS: shipbuilding plate forming by line heating, railway/bridge weld straightening, glass annealing and tempering stress theory (Narayanaswamy-Gardon 1970s structural-relaxation models of residual stress formation), continuous casting and strip-rolling residual-stress control, electron-beam welding distortion work. TRAP: AM residual-stress modelling is crowded and the inherent-strain method is already borrowed, so a lead must be a specific pre-1985 CONTROL strategy with design rules (tensioning levels, heat-sink spacing, pre-stress magnitudes, line-heating recipes) not yet tried in AM, plus a check that the powder bed, layerwise build and build-plate constraint do not kill it. targets.problem: Pulse oximeters over-read SpO2 in darkly pigmented skin, worst in the clinically decisive <80% range. Every current mitigation proposal estimates the melanin term from OUTSIDE the optical path actually used for the saturation calculation (a separate RGB/melanometer reflectance reading, a skin-tone covariate in the calibration regression, or an LED-linewidth correction). The specific stuck sub-question: can the melanin/non-blood absorbance term be measured IN the same optical path, on the same subject, at the same two wavelengths, by acquiring a per-subject blood-free (compression-exsanguinated or cuff-occluded) DC baseline, and does subtracting that measured baseline instead of estimating it remove the pigment-dependent bias?
targets.notes:
The pre-1970 absolute oximetry corpus did exactly this and then it was discarded. Earl Wood's ear oximeter (US Pat. 2,706,927; Wood & Geraci, 1940s-50s; lineage Millikan 1942, Squire 1940) carried a pneumatic pressure capsule that squeezed blood out of the earlobe to take a 'bloodless' two-wavelength blank. Everything remaining in that blank is non-blood tissue absorbance -- melanin included -- measured on that subject, in that path. Subtracting it is what gave the instrument an ABSOLUTE calibration rather than an empirical curve. The abandonment reason is commercial and documented, not scientific: Aoyagi's pulse-ratio method (1974 onward) got rid of the capsule, the operator step and the calibration, by normalizing the AC pulse against the DC level. But that normalization is precisely what throws the pigment term away -- DC is divided out rather than measured, and the ratio-of-ratios is then NOT pigment-immune, because melanin attenuates the red channel far more than infrared (a Monte Carlo result: melanin absorbance at 660 nm is hundreds of times that of blood- and melanin-free tissue), shifts the effective photon path length, and reweights the polychromatic LED emission spectrum (the 2024 BJA mechanism). So the modern field is trying to reconstruct, by proxy, a quantity a 1950s instrument measured directly.

MECHANISTIC REASON THE GAP IS REAL (not merely uncited): the two eras need different vocabularies for the same physical quantity. Wood's corpus calls it the 'bloodless blank' / 'tissue blank' / 'cuvette blank' of an ABSOLUTE non-pulsatile oximeter; the modern corpus calls it the 'DC term', 'pigment bias', or 'melanin compensation factor' of a PULSATILE ratiometric oximeter. A modern literature search on melanin correction never surfaces a 1950s paper about cuvette blanks. And the only reason the old step was dropped is that it required a mechanical compression actuator and a two-phase measurement -- a cost/usability tradeoff, which modern wearables with existing actuators or an inflatable digit cuff can now pay.

What the comb should look for: (1) the full Wood / Millikan / Squire / Brinkman-Zijlstra absolute-oximetry corpus on how the bloodless blank was taken, how long the ear had to be compressed, how the residual blood volume error was bounded, and how much of the inter-subject variance the blank actually removed (the HP 47201A ear oximeter, a 1970s commercial descendant, was advertised as accurate 'regardless of skin pigmentation' -- find the internal validation behind that claim, HP Journal Oct 1976 is a lead); (2) the known failure modes the old corpus already documented, which bound the idea honestly: the 'bloodless' ear is not truly bloodless, compression itself changes the tissue's optical scattering, and any surface site fails in shock/vasoconstriction; (3) whether the residual-blood and compression-optics errors were ever quantified well enough to say what accuracy ceiling a measured blank can reach.

CHEAP VERIFICATION (physical coherence checked): fully computational/benchtop, no new human hypoxia study needed. Step 1 -- on a bench finger/ear phantom with controlled melanin-equivalent absorber layers and a pump-driven pulsatile blood channel, acquire red/IR DC with the blood channel drained vs filled, and test whether the drained blank predicts the known absorber concentration and whether subtracting it collapses the ratio-of-ratios curves measured across absorber levels onto one curve. This is physically coherent: the quantity being isolated is the static non-blood attenuation at the two LED wavelengths, which is present and measurable in both phases, and the drained state is directly realizable in a phantom with none of the in-vivo residual-blood ambiguity. Step 2 -- in vivo, a digit cuff inflated above systolic plus a brief venous-emptying elevation is the human analogue; compare the measured blank against a melanometer reading on the same digit (the Commun Med 2024 melanometry best-practice paper gives the reference method) and ask which better predicts each subject's SpO2 bias in the public OpenOximetry dataset paradigm. Step 2 is the weaker leg because the cuffed digit is not truly bloodless -- that is exactly the limitation the old corpus wrote down, and it should be treated as a known constraint, not a surprise.

IMPORTANT SCOPE NOTE: this is a measurement-physics hypothesis. It is not clinical guidance, and nothing here is a protocol for use on patients.

targets.problem: In the constant-rate CSF infusion test, resistance to outflow (R_out) is recovered reliably but CEREBROSPINAL COMPLIANCE/ELASTANCE is not: compliance parameters 'agreed poorly between methods (R2 = 0.3-0.7) and varied considerably within the observed infusion periods', while R_out converged to within +/-10% in 10-15 min. The specific stuck sub-question: is the poor identifiability of compliance an intrinsic property of the physiology, or an artifact of fitting a plateau-approach model to a transient in which the measurement system's own storage and the pressure-dependence of compliance are not separated -- and do the diagnostic tools built for exactly this identifiability problem in subsurface pressure-transient testing (log-log pressure-derivative diagnostic plots, explicit instrument-storage models, rate-history deconvolution, pseudopressure transforms for stress-sensitive storage) recover compliance from infusion traces that current plateau/ODE fitting cannot?
targets.notes:
The two fields are solving the same inverse problem with different words. A constant-rate CSF infusion is a constant-rate injection test into a compliant, leaky compartment with a fixed outflow conductance and an instrument (catheter + transducer + tubing) that has its own compliance in series. The subsurface well-test literature calls the identical quantities STORATIVITY (= compliance), TRANSMISSIVITY/PERMEABILITY (= 1/R_out), WELLBORE STORAGE (= catheter/system compliance, which dominates exactly the early-time window where compliance information lives), and STRESS-SENSITIVE / PRESSURE-DEPENDENT STORAGE (= the elastance term E that makes compliance fall as ICP rises). That field spent 1950-2005 on the specific failure mode the CSF literature now reports: early-time storage and late-time conductance are strongly correlated in a single constant-rate test, so naive curve-fitting trades one off against the other and the storage estimate is the one that goes unstable. Their answers were (a) Bourdet's log-log pressure-derivative diagnostic plot (1983), which makes the storage-dominated and conductance-dominated regimes visually separable and tells you which part of the trace may legitimately be fitted for which parameter; (b) explicit deconvolution of the instrument/storage response (von Schroeter & Levitan, early 2000s) so that imperfect, non-constant and interrupted rate histories can still be inverted -- directly relevant because the CSF literature already notes 'it is not necessary that the ICP reaches a plateau'; (c) pseudopressure transforms that linearize a system whose storage depends on pressure.

MECHANISTIC REASON THE GAP IS REAL: vocabulary non-overlap in both directions, plus a disciplinary firewall (petroleum/hydrogeology journals vs neurosurgery journals, no shared indexing terms). Nothing in the clinical phrase 'cerebrospinal compliance' retrieves 'storativity', and a derivative-diagnostic paper about a well does not index on 'hydrocephalus'. The CSF field independently rediscovered the physics as poroelasticity (which IS cited in brain modelling), but poroelastic FORWARD simulation is a different tool from well-test INVERSE diagnostics -- a poroelastic infusion-test simulation paper concludes that with arterial pulsations plus nonlinear compliance 'solutions have to be interpreted very carefully to predict parameter values', which is a statement of the identifiability problem, not a method for it.

What the comb should look for: Bourdet/Gringarten derivative-diagnostic methodology; Agarwal-Al-Hussainy-Ramey and the wellbore-storage deconvolution line; the groundwater slug-test and leaky-aquifer (Hantush-Jacob) analogues, which are closer to CSF scale than oilfield cases; and specifically the well-test literature's own quantitative statements about HOW MUCH of the early-time trace must be free of instrument storage before storativity is identifiable -- that number translates directly into a design constraint on infusion-test catheters and sampling rate.

CHEAP VERIFICATION (physical coherence checked): purely retrospective and computational. Take existing archived constant-rate infusion-test pressure traces (the Cambridge/Umea computerised infusion datasets are the obvious source; the Czosnyka computerised method is the incumbent comparator), and (1) replot each as a log-log pressure-derivative diagnostic, (2) test whether the derivative plot separates an early instrument/compartment-storage regime from a later outflow-dominated regime, (3) refit compliance using only the window the diagnostic licenses, plus a deconvolution of the known catheter/transducer compliance, and (4) ask whether between-method agreement for compliance improves on the published R2 = 0.3-0.7 benchmark while R_out estimates stay unchanged (the latter is the negative control -- if R_out moves, the reanalysis is wrong). Physical coherence: the analogy requires only linear-in-the-small storage plus conductance plus a series instrument capacitance, all of which demonstrably exist in the CSF infusion setup; and where the CSF system is nonlinear (compliance falling with pressure above a reference), the well-test toolkit's own pseudopressure/stress-sensitive machinery is the designated tool rather than an assumption being violated. The one real mismatch to state up front: the CSF trace carries large arterial and respiratory pulsations that have no well-test counterpart, so a derivative plot must be computed on a low-pass-filtered trace, and that filtering choice is itself a parameter that has to be reported.

targets.problem: Zero-heat-flux (ZHF) cutaneous thermometry is accurate at thermal steady state but fails during exactly the episodes that matter: on cardiopulmonary bypass, ZHF-vs-nasopharyngeal limits of agreement 'exceeded the clinically acceptable +/- 0.5 degC during CPB-cooling and CPB-rewarming, reaching up to +/- 2.3 degC', with ZHF tracking a visibly slower rate of change than the reference. The specific stuck sub-question: is that transient error a fixed, identifiable dynamic response of the sensor-plus-skin system -- and therefore invertible offline from the ZHF trace alone by the dynamic-compensation methods built for slow heat-flux and embedded-thermocouple sensors in thermal engineering -- or is it, as the clinical literature currently asserts, irreducibly physiological?
targets.notes:
ZHF thermometry is a NULL method by construction: a servo heater drives the flux through an insulating pad to zero so the skin surface equilibrates with deep tissue, and the reading is then taken as core. Nulling is intrinsically a steady-state operation; the system's approach to null is governed by the thermal mass and conductance of pad plus skin plus perfused subcutis, so during a forced transient the output is necessarily a lagged, low-pass-filtered, amplitude-attenuated version of the true deep temperature. The clinical field treats this as a nuisance to be excluded (studies carve out cooling/rewarming phases) or as physiology. The most on-point 2026 CPB paper explicitly attributes the lag to 'physiological delays in thermal equilibration rather than limitations inherent to the zero-heat-flux technique' -- that attribution is a falsifiable claim, and it is the claim this target attacks, because a first-order or two-node lumped sensor-plus-tissue model predicts the same qualitative signature (slower rate of change, growing offset in the direction of the ramp, offset that decays after the ramp stops) with no physiology invoked at all.

The old/other corpus: thermal-engineering transient thermometry, which has treated 'my sensor is slower than the thing I am measuring' as a solved inverse problem for decades -- dynamic error correction of thermocouples and heat-flux gauges posed as an inverse heat conduction problem, embedded-thermocouple correction transfer functions (a 2005 thesis line, dynamically correcting installation-induced bias via an embedded-thermocouple correction transfer function), and the whole regularization literature for the resulting ill-posed deconvolution (Tikhonov, and more recent filtered-kernel regularization inside physics-informed networks reporting ~0.83% peak relative error vs 2.05-2.2% for older schemes). That corpus also supplies the thing the clinical field has never measured: a response time.

MECHANISTIC REASON THE GAP IS REAL: different vocabularies for the same physical quantity, plus opposite framings of the same artifact. The engineering field says 'sensor time constant / dynamic error / inverse heat conduction'; the clinical field says 'time lag for establishing temperature equilibrium' and 'isothermal tunnel formation' and then handles it STATISTICALLY -- the CPB paper's own time adjustment is 'residuals from linear regressions on time, not a physical model of sensor response'. A regression on time cannot invert a convolution, so the correction being applied is categorically the wrong class of tool for the artifact being corrected. There is also a device-design reason the gap persisted: ZHF was commercialized as a single-number display, so the raw heater power and dual-thermistor signals that a deconvolution needs are not exposed by the clinical products -- a documented-in-hardware barrier, not a scientific one.

What the comb should look for: the Gardon-gauge / thin-film heat-flux-sensor dynamic calibration corpus; inverse-heat-conduction deconvolution with regularization; embedded-thermocouple correction transfer functions and how their time constants were identified experimentally (step response in a stirred bath); and critically, whether that corpus already establishes the identifiability limits -- how much sensor noise destroys a deconvolution at a given ramp rate -- since those limits set whether a 1-2 degC/min CPB ramp is recoverable at all.

CHEAP VERIFICATION (physical coherence checked): three cheap legs, in order of cost. (1) Bench, no subjects: mount a ZHF pad on a perfused skin-equivalent phantom or a water-jacketed gel block, drive the block through step and ramp changes spanning CPB rates, and identify the sensor-plus-pad transfer function (time constant(s), DC gain). This simply measures the number the clinical literature has never reported -- the Europe PMC sweep found 'No record explicitly measures response time or lag of a ZHF sensor.' (2) Retrospective, computational: take already-published paired ZHF-vs-nasopharyngeal traces from CPB cooling/rewarming and test whether a one- or two-time-constant deconvolution with the bench-identified constants tightens the limits of agreement toward +/- 0.5 degC. Negative control: the same deconvolution must NOT degrade agreement during the thermally steady phases, where mean bias is already small (-0.55 to 0.28 degC). (3) If (1) and (2) hold, the strong test: does a ZHF trace plus deconvolution predict the direction and magnitude of the error during the rewarming ramp, where the clinical paper measured TZHF rising relative to TNP to about 0.53 degC by the end -- a signed, specific number to hit.

Physical coherence: the imported method operates on a linear(izable) lumped thermal system driven below its own bandwidth, which is precisely the ZHF regime during a slow surgical ramp, so there is no regime where the old technique cannot function. The honest constraints: the ill-posedness means noise is amplified by differentiation, so leg (2) depends on sampling rate and quantization of the archived traces (clinical monitors often log at low rates and 0.1 degC resolution -- if so, deconvolution may be infeasible on legacy data and leg (1) plus a prospective high-rate recording is required); and perfusion changes DO modulate the tissue conductance, so the transfer function is not strictly time-invariant -- the test is whether a fixed-parameter deconvolution captures enough of the artifact to matter, not whether it is exact.

SCOPE NOTE: this is an instrumentation-physics hypothesis for device researchers. It is not clinical guidance and prescribes nothing for patient management.

targets.problem: Multi-site replication projects in psychology and experimental social science (Many Labs, Registered Replication Reports) need to decide whether observed between-site spread in an effect size reflects real moderation by sample/setting or merely a few badly-behaved sites. Current practice estimates a single random-effects tau (plus I-squared) per effect, an approach known to be badly biased downward and poorly calibrated when the number of sites is ~20-60. The specific stuck sub-question: with k sites each measuring the same pre-registered protocol, how do you (a) separate within-site imprecision from between-site location shift, and (b) identify WHICH sites are discrepant in location versus in scatter, with a calibrated decision rule? Analytical chemistry and physical metrology solved exactly this problem between 1950 and 1994 and standardised the solution as ISO 5725-2 and ASTM E691: repeatability/reproducibility variance decomposition, Mandel's h statistic (per-lab location consistency) and Mandel's k statistic (per-lab scatter consistency) with tabulated critical values, Youden two-sample plots to separate systematic from random lab error, and ISO 13528 robust consensus-value estimation with z-scores. The hypothesis: porting this machinery to multi-site replication data yields per-site diagnostics and a site-outlier decision rule that the current random-effects workflow does not provide at all.

MODERN REVIEW FETCHED AND REFERENCE LIST CHECKED: arXiv:1710.06031, 'Large Scale Replication Projects in Contemporary Psychological Research' (the most on-point methods critique of how multi-site replication projects analyse between-site variability). Result of checking its bibliography for metrology/ISO/ASTM/Mandel/Youden/measurement-science entries: "None of the references concern metrology, ISO, ASTM, Mandel, Youden, or physical/chemical measurement science." The three nearest entries are Klein et al. 2014 (Many Labs), Lindsay & Ehrenberg 1993 'The design of replicated studies', and Ehrenberg & Bound 1993 -- all psychology/statistics. What the paper proposes instead: a hierarchical multilevel model with partial pooling, I-squared with Pigott (2012) 25/50/75 percent thresholds, post-stratification (Park et al. 2004; Kennedy & Gelman 2018). It explicitly criticises the two-parameter random-effects model and the zero-heterogeneity test as "poorly calibrated when the number of laboratories is small" and cites Chung et al. (2013a,b) on downward bias -- i.e. it diagnoses precisely the problem ISO 5725-2 variance components and Mandel h/k address, and reaches for none of it.

WHY THE GAP HAS A STRUCTURAL REASON (not merely 'nobody cited it'): (1) Vocabulary split -- metrology fixes 'repeatability' and 'reproducibility' as technical terms for within- and between-laboratory precision (ISO 5725-1/-2, VIM); psychology uses 'reproducibility' and 'replicability' with the opposite-ish and contested meanings, so a keyword search from either side misses the other. (2) Publication-venue split -- the core corpus is ISO/ASTM/IUPAC standards documents and the NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook, which are paywalled standards or grey literature, NOT journal articles, so they are largely absent from citation indices that social scientists search. (3) Mandel's own papers are in Journal of Quality Technology / Materials Research & Standards, 1960s-70s, not indexed alongside psychology.

  Dataset: Many Labs 2 (Klein et al. 2018, AMPPS 1(4):443-490, doi 10.1177/2515245918810225). Public repository osf.io/8cd4r (confirmed live; its wiki documents the 28 findings and the preregistered design and carries a July 2019 correction note). A ready-made site-level extract exists on CRAN: psymetadata::manylabs2018 -- confirmed 1,414 rows, 23 variables, including a `lab` site identifier and effect sizes in both r and Cohen's d, sourced from osf.io/ux3eh. Note the raw participant-level ML2 data contains PII and is restricted, so use the aggregated site-level file. Supplementary: the Registered Replication Reports (e.g. Alogna et al. verbal overshadowing) for a second, smaller k.
  Estimator: ISO 5725-2 one-way random-effects variance decomposition into s_r (repeatability) and s_R (reproducibility), then Mandel's h (standardised between-site deviation of each site mean from the grand mean) and Mandel's k (ratio of each site's within-site SD to the pooled within-site SD), with ASTM E691 critical values. Both are implemented and installable today: PMCMRplus::mandelhTest and PMCMRplus::mandelkTest (documented as implementing ASTM E691) and metRology::mandel.kh. Add ISO 13528 robust consensus value (Algorithm A) and per-site z-scores. Because each ML2 site ran many of the 28 effects, the Youden two-sample plot applies directly with two effects per site.
  Falsifiable outcome: run Mandel h/k on each of the 28 ML2 effects and ask whether the flagged sites concentrate on particular labs across effects. If a small number of sites are flagged repeatedly across unrelated effects, that is site-level systematic error (a lab property), which the per-effect random-effects tau structurally cannot see because it is fit one effect at a time -- and it would partially undercut the ML2 headline conclusion that variability 'was attributable more to the effect being studied than to the sample or setting'. If flags are scattered at the nominal rate, the import is genuinely null and the target closes cheaply.
